parts: Rise of the West and British control

From 1450 the printing press, the Renaissance and Reformation and new trade routes changed Europe, which progressed in science, exploration and gunnery. The Portuguese, Dutch, French and finally the British competed for Indian trade; the British gained trade, then the country and drained its wealth. They used the many states that arose after the Mughal decline, setting one ruler against another; Tipu Sultan of Mysore tried to use the French–British rivalry but could not match their diplomacy and fire power. British domination had three phases: control of trade (buying cheap from peasants through Seths and gomastas), control of production to suit exports and destruction of Indian industries, and intensified imperialism for British economic interests. After the Battle of Plassey (1757) they became the real masters of Bengal, monopolised raw cotton and imposed heavy duties on Indian goods in Britain. With the industrial revolution Indian handicrafts lost home and foreign markets by 1813, when the Company's monopoly ended and India became an economic colony: an excellent consumer of British goods and a supplier of raw materials. Steamships, railways (first line Bombay to Thane, 1853) and the telegraph and postal service (Dalhousie, Calcutta to Agra, 1853) served British commerce but also brought Indians and ideas closer.

Agriculture was the main occupation but constant war prevented improvement. Foreign trade flourished under the Mughals (imports: pearls, raw silk, wool, dates from the Persian Gulf; coffee, gold, drugs, honey from Arabia; tea, porcelain, silk from China; luxury goods from Tibet, Singapore, Indonesia, Africa and Europe; exports: raw silk, silk fabrics, indigo, sugar, pepper and famous cotton textiles). Despite a favourable balance of trade, the economy suffered from constant warfare, revolts of Sikhs, Jats and Marathas, and invasions by Nadir Shah (1739) and Ahmad Shah Abdali (1761). Socially there was division on region, tribe, language and caste; caste rules governed marriage, diet, inter-dining and profession; science and mathematics were neglected; education was traditional, supported by local rulers and the rich, and girls seldom went to school. Hindu–Muslim relations were friendly with tolerance and shared festivals.

Women's condition was poor: the birth of a girl was thought unfortunate, child marriage and polygamy were common, there was no right to property or divorce, perpetual widowhood for upper castes (widows could not wear coloured clothes or attend marriages, their presence being inauspicious), purdah, and no education. Christian missionaries opened schools and started the printing press; English education opened the window to liberalism, rationalism, democracy, equality and freedom, and English became the lingua franca of the educated. Ram Mohan Roy, harbinger of the modern age, had Sati banned and founded the Brahmo Samaj (monotheism, against idol worship, polytheism and ritualism); Debendranath Tagore and Keshab Chandra Sen followed; it was the first organised vehicle of national awakening. Prarthana Samaj (Bombay, 1867, Dr Atmaram Pandurang; Ranade): inter-caste dining and marriage, widow remarriage, uplift of women and depressed classes. Ramakrishna Paramhansa and Vivekananda (Ramakrishna Mission): equality and oneness of religions, Vedanta. Theosophical Society (Madame Blavatsky, Colonel Olcott; Annie Besant founded the Central Hindu School). Narayana Guru (born Kerala 1854) worked for social and religious reform. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan started the Aligarh movement and the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College (later Aligarh Muslim University), against purdah, polygamy and easy divorce, giving Muslims Urdu and a press. Swami Dayanand founded the Arya Samaj in 1875 ('go back to the Vedas', Satyartha Prakash, Shuddhi movement, DAV schools from 1886). Jyotiba Phule (Pune, born 1827): school for lower castes and the Satya Shodhak Samaj (1873). Pandita Ramabai: Sharda Sadan, a home for widows (1890). Maharshi Karve (Bharat Ratna) worked for women's education; the Sharda Act (passed 1929, in force 1930) set minimum marriage age at 18 for boys and 14 for girls. Ambedkar and Gandhi worked for the depressed classes (Gandhi: Harijans).

Lithography (invented 1798) allowed many copies; from about 1820 hundreds of pamphlets and books appeared, and the press became a powerful tool of public opinion and nationalism. Novels, essays and poems in Indian languages stirred nationalism: Bankim Chandra's Anandamath, Dinabandhu Mitra's Neeldarpan, Bhartendu Harishchandra's Bharat Durdasha, Lakshminath Bezbaruah (Assamese), Subramania Bharati (Tamil) and Altaf Hussain Hali (Urdu). Newspapers: Hindoo Patriot, Amrita Bazar Patrika (Bengal), Maharatha and Kesari (Bombay), The Hindu and Swadeshamitran (Madras), The Tribune, Akhbar-i-Am (Punjab).

The Indian National Congress was founded by A.O. Hume in 1885 (era of Moderates); the Muslim League was seen as the first fruit of 'divide and rule'. Home Rule Leagues (1915–16) were started by Tilak at Poona and Annie Besant at Madras. 1905–18 was the era of Extremists (Lal, Bal, Pal) with agitation against Curzon's partition of Bengal, Boycott and Swadeshi. 1919–34: Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919, General Dyer), Khilafat and Non-cooperation under Gandhi (his first triumph was the Champaran Satyagraha), Swaraj Party, Simon Commission, Nehru Report (1928), Purna Swaraj at Lahore (1929), Salt Satyagraha or Dandi March (6 April 1930) and Civil Disobedience. Government of India Act 1935; Quit India (August 1942) after the Cripps Mission; INA (Azad Hind Fauj) of Subhas Chandra Bose (1943); Cabinet Mission 1946; India became free on 15 August 1947 after partition. Independent India built a secular democratic republic, integrated the princely states and began economic planning.
